posts.title: Why I Made This Little Corner of the Internet
posts.excerpt: I wanted a small place on the internet that is actually mine — a place for ideas, experiments, things I'm learning, and thoughts worth keeping.
posts.content:
I have always liked the idea of having a small place on the internet that is actually mine.

Not a profile. Not a feed. Not a place where an algorithm decides what deserves attention. Just a website, sitting somewhere on the internet, with my name on it.

I made this blog for the things that don't have an obvious place to go.

Ideas I can't stop thinking about. Things I'm building. Things I'm learning. Experiments that work, experiments that fail, and the strange things I discover somewhere in between. Sometimes it might be technology. Sometimes it might be a project. Sometimes it might be an observation that would never be worth turning into a social media post.

And sometimes it might be nothing particularly important at all.

I don't want this to become a content machine.

I don't want to have to publish every Tuesday. I don't want to write something just because the calendar says I should. And I don't want to turn every thought into a lesson, a thread, a headline, or something designed to get attention.

I just want a place to write.

The internet once felt a little more like this to me. People made websites because they wanted to make websites. They wrote because they had something to say. They built strange little projects, experimented with ideas, and left pieces of themselves scattered across the web.

I miss that feeling.

So this is my attempt to make a small version of it.

This blog is a place for me to think in public, build in public, and keep a record of where my mind has been.

Some posts might be carefully thought out. Others might be messy. Some ideas might turn into something bigger. Others might disappear after I write them down.

That's fine.

Not everything needs to become something.

Maybe nobody reads some of these posts. Honestly, that's okay too.

Because there is another reason I'm writing them.

One day, years from now, I might come back here and read something written by the person I am today. I might disagree with him. I might laugh at him. I might wonder why he ever thought that way.

But I'll know him.

I'll be able to see what I was thinking, what I was trying to build, what I cared about, and what I didn't yet understand.

Maybe that's what this place is really for.

Not an audience.

A record.

A little corner of the internet where I can leave things behind.

Anyway, welcome.

This is mine.

Let's see where it goes.

posts.title: Steve Jobs: The University of Universities of Marketing
posts.excerpt: When I think about Steve Jobs, I don't just think about technology. I think about marketing, presentation, the power of an idea, and the man I consider the university of universities of marketing.
posts.content:
Whenever I think about Steve Jobs, the first thing that comes to my mind is not simply Apple, the iPhone, the Mac, or the famous presentations. What interests me the most about him is the way he understood marketing. In my opinion, Steve Jobs was not just a businessman or a technology person. For me, he was almost like the university of universities of marketing. The way he presented an idea, created curiosity around a product, and made people emotionally interested in something was on another level.

And that is what makes Steve Jobs so interesting to me.

We live in a world where companies constantly tell us about specifications. More RAM. Better processor. Bigger battery. Better camera. Faster performance. More features. But Steve Jobs understood that simply telling people what a product has is not always enough. You have to make people understand why that product matters. You have to make them interested in the idea behind it.

That is the part of Steve Jobs that I find most impressive.

## More than a technology company

When I look at Apple and the products that came out under Steve Jobs, I don't see it only as a technology story. I see it as a story of presentation, perception and marketing as well.

Steve Jobs understood how to put an idea in front of people.

And perhaps that's why his product launches became so memorable. A product could be technically complicated behind the scenes, but the way it was presented to an ordinary person could be incredibly simple. Instead of making the audience feel that they needed to understand technology, the presentation made them feel that they simply needed to understand the possibility.

That, to me, is powerful marketing.

## The man behind many things we hold today

Another reason I find Steve Jobs interesting is the scale of his influence. Many of the technologies and products that are now completely normal parts of our lives were shaped by the companies and products he helped build.

Today, we hold smartphones in our hands without thinking much about how unusual that idea once was. We use computers, digital music, graphical interfaces and countless other technologies as if they have always existed in their current form.

But people like Steve Jobs played a major role in taking technology from something that could feel complicated and technical and turning it into something people wanted to use.

And I think that distinction matters.

Creating technology is one thing.

Making millions of ordinary people want that technology is another.

## This is why I call him the university of universities of marketing

I don't use that phrase casually.

When I say Steve Jobs was the university of universities of marketing, I mean that there is something to learn from the way he communicated an idea. He understood that a product doesn't exist only because engineers built it. A product also exists in the mind of the person looking at it.

How does the customer see it?

What does the product represent to them?

Why would they care?

Why would they remember it?

Why would they talk about it?

These questions can be just as important as the technical specifications.

And this is something I find particularly relevant today because almost everyone can create something. We have tools, technology and artificial intelligence that allow us to build things much faster than before. But building something and making people care about what you built are completely different challenges.

Steve Jobs understood the second part exceptionally well.

## I'm not saying he was perfect

I also don't think appreciating Steve Jobs means we have to treat everything about him as perfect.

He was a human being, not a fictional character.

There are many things written and discussed about his personality, his management style and the way he treated people. Those things are part of his story too. I don't think success automatically makes every decision a person makes correct.

For me, the point of studying someone like Steve Jobs isn't to blindly copy him.

It is to understand what he did exceptionally well.

And for me, one of those things is unquestionably marketing.

## What I actually take from Steve Jobs

The biggest thing I take from Steve Jobs is not that everyone should build another Apple.

It is that an idea becomes much more powerful when you know how to communicate it.

You can have a brilliant idea sitting inside your notebook. You can have an amazing product sitting inside your computer. You can have something genuinely useful. But if you cannot make another person understand its value, the idea may never go anywhere.

That is why I find Steve Jobs so fascinating.

He showed that innovation isn't only about creating something.

It is also about how you introduce that creation to the world.

And perhaps that is why, whenever I think about Steve Jobs, I don't just think about technology.

I think about marketing.

I think about presentation.

I think about the power of an idea.

And I think about a person who, in my view, became something much bigger than just a successful businessman.

For me, Steve Jobs was the university of universities of marketing.

## A note to the reader

This article represents my personal views and opinions about Steve Jobs. The wording and structure of this article were generated with the help of ChatGPT, but the opinions presented as my views are based on what I have personally expressed. ChatGPT was used as a writing and editing tool, not as the source of my opinions.

posts.title: Happy Birthday Doraemon!
posts.excerpt: Some things from childhood never really leave us. For me, Doraemon is one of those things — a character, a world, and a memory that I still carry with me.
posts.content:
There are some things from childhood that you don't really grow out of.

You just grow older, and somehow they stay with you.

For me, Doraemon is one of those things.

Today is September 3, and it is Doraemon's birthday. His official birth date is September 3, 2112, which is still more than a hundred years from now. Funny, isn't it? A character who technically belongs to the future has been such a big part of our childhood and our past.

I have been watching Doraemon since I was a kid. I remember waiting for it on television. Waiting for the episode. Waiting for the songs. Waiting to see what Nobita had done this time and what Doraemon was going to pull out of that pocket.

At that time, I never thought about any of it this deeply.

It was just Doraemon.

And maybe that's what made it so special.

You didn't need a reason to watch it. You just wanted to.

Nobita was always getting into trouble. He would come running to Doraemon, ask for some crazy gadget, and for a few minutes everything would seem perfect. Then, as usual, things would go completely out of control.

And we loved it.

Because somewhere, Nobita was also us.

Not because we were exactly like him, but because we knew what it felt like to be scared, to fail, to be lazy sometimes, to want an easy way out, or simply to wish that someone would come and fix everything.

And Doraemon was that someone.

But the more I think about it now, the more I realise that Doraemon's gadgets were never the real reason we loved the show.

It was the friendship.

Doraemon could get angry with Nobita. He could shout at him, get irritated with him and tell him not to misuse the gadgets. But whenever Nobita really needed him, Doraemon was there.

Then there was Shizuka, Gian and Suneo. They all had their own personalities, their own problems and their own way of being friends. Together, they made that little world feel complete.

And then came the movies.

I don't think I can explain properly how much I loved Doraemon movies.

The stories suddenly became bigger. The adventures went far beyond their neighbourhood. Time, space, history, different worlds, strange creatures, impossible situations—everything became possible.

But what made those movies different was that they never felt like they were trying too hard.

They could make you laugh in one scene and genuinely emotional in another.

And the music.

Honestly, Doraemon's music deserves its own conversation.

Some of those background tunes and songs have stayed somewhere in my head for years. Sometimes you hear a particular melody and suddenly you are not just listening to music anymore. You are back in front of the television, watching Doraemon as a kid.

That's the strange thing about childhood.

You don't realise that you are living through memories while they are happening.

You realise it much later.

Doraemon first appeared as a manga in December 1969, created by Hiroshi Fujimoto under the name Fujiko F. Fujio. The series was then serialized in Shogakukan's school magazines from 1970. What started as a manga eventually became a world known across generations.

And behind that world was a person who imagined all of it.

Fujiko F. Fujio passed away on September 23, 1996. But there is something beautiful about the fact that his work never really stopped living. The Fujiko F. Fujio Museum describes the ideas behind his work through things like dreams, hope, friendship, courage, curiosity and affection for people.

I think that is exactly why Doraemon lasted.

It wasn't only about a robot cat from the future.

It was about imagination.

It was about friendship.

It was about having someone beside you when things went wrong.

It was about believing that maybe, somehow, tomorrow could be a little better.

And today, when I look at Doraemon from a little distance, I realise something else.

I don't think I miss only the cartoon.

I miss the version of myself who used to watch it.

The kid who could sit in front of the TV and genuinely get excited because Doraemon was about to start.

The kid who didn't care how many times he had already watched an episode.

The kid who could hear a familiar song and instantly feel happy.

That kid has grown up.

But he isn't completely gone.

Maybe that's what Doraemon gives us even today—a small way back to that part of ourselves.

So today, on September 3, I just want to say—

Happy Birthday, Doraemon.

And thank you, Fujiko F. Fujio, for creating something that travelled much further than you could have imagined.

You created a character for children.

But you also created memories for adults.

And somewhere in those memories is a little boy named Shashank, sitting in front of a television, waiting for Doraemon to begin.

Maybe that's why this birthday feels personal.

Because Doraemon wasn't just something I watched.

Doraemon is a part of my childhood that I still carry with me.

And I think I always will.
